PullRequest.Title: Update bundled DOMPurify to 3.4.17
PullRequest.Body:
Update the vendored DOMPurify copy used by VS Code and Monaco (`src/vs/base/browser/dompurify/`) from 3.4.16 to 3.4.17.

This copy is what `monaco-editor-core`, and therefore monaco-editor, ships. DOMPurify 3.4.16 and older are affected by the following public advisories, all fixed in 3.4.17. Security scanners flag downstream Monaco consumers for them:

- [GHSA-cg2g-xh64-v4q7](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-cg2g-xh64-v4q7) (critical)
- [GHSA-mrv2-3pqr-j5jr](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mrv2-3pqr-j5jr) (high)
- [GHSA-c6gr-qvv4-5v3f](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c6gr-qvv4-5v3f) (low)

## Changes
- Replace the bundled ESM implementation (`dist/purify.es.mjs`) and TypeScript declarations (`dist/purify.es.d.mts`) with the official DOMPurify 3.4.17 distribution.
- Update the component manifest version, tag, and upstream commit to `a77a3e78b59f72fa4d1c83f22e121ad9cc7d3575` (tag `3.4.17`).
- Keep omitting the source-map reference because the map is not vendored. The upstream license text is unchanged between 3.4.16 and 3.4.17, so the vendored license notice is unchanged.

Related: https://github.com/microsoft/monaco-editor/issues/5454. It should remain open until a Monaco release containing this update is published. This PR does not assess whether any particular advisory is exploitable in VS Code.

## Validation
- npm package SHA-512 integrity verified (`sha512-B/pSlYVHQ58kqISD/yDjuJ1yfzI34m1gF4lAod2bwSRhiN4K5Cl3H8Af7hqB2PmTL911tdEudnnXn5FnhRoz0w==`). The committed implementation is byte-identical to `purify.es.mjs` minus the source-map comment; the declarations are byte-identical to `purify.es.d.mts`.
- Runtime version (`DOMPurify.version === "3.4.17"`) and manifest provenance (tag `3.4.17` dereferences to `a77a3e78b59f`, the package's `gitHead`) verified.
- `dompurify@3.4.17` is available in the authenticated build feed used by the Monaco release, and that feed serves a byte-identical tarball.
- `pnpm run build-fast --client-only` passed.
- `node test/unit/browser/index.js --browser chromium --run src/vs/base/test/browser/domSanitize.test.ts --run src/vs/base/test/browser/markdownRenderer.test.ts`: 208 passing, 2 pending.
- `tsc --project src/tsconfig.json --noEmit --skipLibCheck` and `tsc --project src/tsconfig.monaco.json --noEmit` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The public declaration explicitly supports `IN_PLACE` as the faster node-sanitization mode, and the changed synchronous call path and unconditional helper calls establish the added O(N) work directly. Exact wall-clock cost varies by DOM size and browser, which is reflected in low severity; VS Code's in-repository markdown callers use strings, but the vendored Monaco API exposes this path to downstream consumers.
Findings.PerformanceResource: DOM traversal CPU plus arrays and Sets retaining references to O(N) DOM nodes
Findings.PerformanceScaling: The added work and retained references grow linearly with every node in the input tree; in the no-mutation common case all three extra O(N) walks still execute, with no cache, coalescing, or early gate.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: increased synchronous sanitization latency and transient GC pressure
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this diff, `IN_PLACE` did not snapshot every input node, maintain a visited Set, rescan for unvisited originals, or build a final reachable Set; after the existing patch-linkage and shadow-root scans it sanitized the tree and only neutralized subtrees recorded as removed.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Every successful `IN_PLACE` call now performs three additional whole-tree walks and allocates an N-node snapshot, an N-entry visited Set, two temporary N-node arrays, and a reachable-element Set, even when no hook or custom element moves a node.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: RIGHT line 2440 newly snapshots the entire live tree with `_collectLiveNodes(dirty)` immediately after the pre-existing `_neutralizePatchLinkage(dirty)` full-tree sweep. The same diff then adds another `_collectLiveNodes(root)` in `_sanitizeUnvisitedNodes` (reached unconditionally at RIGHT line 2463) and another in `_neutralizeEscapedElements` (reached unconditionally through RIGHT line 2475).
Findings.Title: Coalesce the new whole-tree IN_PLACE bookkeeping
Findings.Impact: A Monaco consumer sanitizing a large existing DOM with `{ IN_PLACE: true }` now blocks the calling/UI thread for roughly twice as many whole-tree traversals and creates several node-sized collections, increasing latency and GC pressure on the exact large-tree use case for which `IN_PLACE` is documented as faster.
Findings.Evidence: For an unchanged N-node tree, the old path already swept `_neutralizePatchLinkage`, scanned for attached shadow roots, and ran the sanitizer iterator. The new path additionally collects all live nodes at entry, marks every sanitized node in a Set, collects the tree again solely to discover whether anything was unvisited, and finally collects it a third time to construct a reachable Set before returning. None of these three added traversals is conditional on actual tree mutation.
Findings.Recommendation: Preserve the mutation hardening but coalesce bookkeeping with existing walks: collect the initial snapshot during the patch-linkage/shadow discovery pass, and have the unvisited/reachability walkers update their boolean/Set directly instead of first materializing full `live` arrays. This removes duplicate traversal/allocation without dropping the final mutation checks.

Scenarios.Scenario: VS Code markdown, notebook, and release-note string sanitization before rendering
Scenarios.CriticalPath: DOMPurify sanitizes synchronously before markdown, notebook output, or release-note HTML can be assigned to the DOM, so sanitizer CPU is on the rendering critical path.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Parsed HTML node and attribute count in each rendered markdown document or notebook output.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Calls are synchronous and serialized on the renderer/UI thread; there is no worker, limiter, queue, or coalescing layer.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No sanitizer result cache is used; each rendered HTML string is parsed and sanitized independently, for both cold and repeated renders.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: call sites, configuration construction, and the `typeof dirty !== "string"` IN_PLACE gate were traced directly.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Markdown size and render frequency vary, but repository callers pass strings and therefore do not enter the new IN_PLACE snapshot/visited/reachability path.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression on this path. The changed sanitizer remains a synchronous O(N) parse/walk; the substantial new repeated-tree bookkeeping is gated off for string inputs, and the remaining per-node changes do not establish a concrete user-visible regression.

Scenarios.Scenario: Monaco/DOMPurify consumers sanitizing an existing DOM node with IN_PLACE enabled
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The public sanitize call completes all tree scans and collection construction synchronously before returning the sanitized node, so every added pass blocks consumer progress.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Total light-DOM and open-shadow-root nodes N, after no deduplication is possible because each node identity is retained; element count controls the final reachable Set.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Single-threaded synchronous DOM work; concurrent callers on the same renderer serialize naturally on the event loop, with no batching or backpressure.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: There is no cache across calls and no reuse of the new node snapshots or Sets; cold and warm calls perform the same bookkeeping.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: Very high: the diff unconditionally adds the entry snapshot, visited Set, unvisited rescan, and final reachability rescan for every successful node input with IN_PLACE enabled.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The repository contains no direct IN_PLACE caller, so downstream Monaco usage and typical DOM sizes are uncertain; the API declaration explicitly exposes and describes this mode, lowering severity rather than confidence in the mechanism.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable low-severity repeated-work regression: the no-mutation common case still adds three O(N) tree walks and multiple O(N) collections on the synchronous call path.

Scenarios.Scenario: First sanitizer-module load in VS Code or Monaco
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Static sanitizer initialization may occur on first import, but it performs only local constructor/getter setup and is not connected to filesystem, network, IPC, or subprocess work.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Fixed-size tables and prototype accessor lookups, independent of document size.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One module evaluation per realm, serialized by the module loader.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Module initialization has no cache-miss cycle beyond JavaScript module singleton evaluation; subsequent imports reuse the evaluated module.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: top-level additions and removals are directly visible in the diff.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: First-import placement varies by bundle and product surface, but the changed fixed-size initialization work is small and does not scale with user content.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable startup regression; the fixed Set/prototype helper setup is bounded, while removal of the per-tag literal-close regex table offsets initialization work.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all three changed files and every implementation diff page. One low-severity IN_PLACE repeated-traversal regression was submitted; string sanitization and module initialization had no high-confidence reportable performance issue.
